You might believe you should spend less time thinking about code because of AI. 

I strongly disagree! We’re watching this play out live where tons of AI generated code becomes a liability.

At the end of the day, an engineer needs to be responsible / on call for code that gets shipped to production. If you don’t understand the system you’re trying to debug, you’re probably going to have a bad time.

Yes, AI can help with all of this, if you set up the proper systems. You can have agents triage prod logs, look at errors, etc. You can speed up parts of the investigation, but an engineer needs to make the call. There might be serious customer or financial implications from that change. 

I expect the trend continue for trimming dependencies, vendoring code so you can modify it directly, preferring simpler systems with fewer abstractions, and spending waaaay more time thinking about system design and code maintenance.

I’ve said this before, but it’s a great time to get familiar with CS fundamentals and some of the history behind what great software looks like. Many parts will be different in the coming years as AI progresses, but also a lot more than people realize will stay the same.

⚡️If a country imports large numbers of people from low-trust, poor, conflict-scarred, clan-based, or weak-state societies into a high-trust welfare democracy, the state is importing more than labor. 

It is importing behavioral distributions, family structures, conflict norms, educational gaps, trauma, religious/cultural differences, sex-ratio distortions, and different relationships to law, women, authority, and public goods.

That changes outcomes.

Europe’s mistake was assuming institutions could absorb unlimited demographic difference without the trust substrate changing. 

That was fantasy. 

High-trust societies are not magic machines. They are inherited behavioral systems. They depend on norms of restraint, reciprocity, low corruption, female safety, social shame, work participation, and legitimacy of law. Import enough people who do not already share those norms, then the receiving society either assimilates them hard or gets changed by them.

Europe mostly chose neither. It chose welfare absorption plus moral denial.

So what did they “gain”?

Short term: labor supply, demographic patching, moral status, cheap service workers, asylum compliance, elite self-image, employer benefits, and a way to avoid confronting birth-rate collapse.

Long term: fragmented cities, welfare pressure, crime overrepresentation in some origin groups, political radicalization, distrust, housing strain, school strain, policing strain, and a far-right backlash that becomes stronger each time the official class lies about the tradeoff.

That is the actual structure.

The biggest lie from the pro-immigration side is pretending origin does not matter. It does. Country of origin often proxies for human capital, culture, war exposure, family structure, trust, religion, education, and integration difficulty.

The policy answer is obvious and politically forbidden: immigration has to be selective, conditional, assimilative, and reversible. Welfare access should not be automatic. Criminality should trigger removal where legally possible. Citizenship should be harder. Family reunification should be narrower. High-skill immigration should be separated from asylum and low-skill welfare migration. Data should be published honestly by origin, generation, sex, age, and offense category.

A country that hides the data has already lost moral authority.

Europe tried to solve demographics and morality with migration while pretending culture was irrelevant. 

The bill is now arriving as crime data, welfare dependence, social distrust, and political revolt.

⚡️AI is going to break the consulting pyramid.

The expensive part of consulting has always been disguised labor arbitrage: 

Armies of smart juniors scraping data, formatting slides, summarizing interviews, benchmarking peers, building models, writing decks, and packaging obvious recommendations in institutional language.

AI attacks that layer directly.

That means clients will keep asking a brutal question: 

Why pay McKinsey rates for work that an internal team with AI can now do 70% as well in 10% of the time?

The top firms survive, but the model changes. McKinsey, Bain, BCG, Deloitte, Accenture, etc. still have value where the product is trust, implementation, politics, regulatory safety, board legitimacy, transformation management, and executive cover. A CEO does not hire McKinsey only for the answer. The CEO hires McKinsey to make the answer institutionally acceptable, politically transferable, and blame-resistant.

That layer remains human.

The junior-deck factory gets repriced.

This is the real fracture: AI commoditizes analysis, but it does not commoditize responsibility.

Clients could always Google ideas. They could always read books. They could always hire smart analysts. The hard part was forcing an organization to act, aligning executives, neutralizing internal resistance, making the board comfortable, and giving leadership a respected outside authority to point at when the decision hurts.

AI can produce advice. It cannot yet walk into a boardroom, absorb institutional risk, fire the sacred cow, manage the politics, own the transformation, and become the ritual scapegoat if things go wrong.

So consulting does not disappear. It unbundles.

Low-end research gets crushed.

Generic strategy decks get crushed.

Benchmarking gets crushed.

Market maps get crushed.

“Best practices” sludge gets crushed.

Implementation, restructuring, regulatory navigation, AI transformation, M&A integration, cybersecurity, supply-chain redesign, cost takeout, and board-level political cover remain valuable.

The real winners are AI-native boutiques that combine senior judgment with machine leverage. 

Ten excellent people plus AI can do what used to require fifty consultants. That destroys the old leverage model because the pyramid depended on billing junior hours at premium rates.

The firms most at risk are mid-tier consultancies with weak brand cover and commodity deliverables. The giants have brand armor. Tiny elite boutiques have specialization. The middle gets squeezed hardest.

Deepest read: AI is exposing that a lot of “expert advice” was just expensive formatting around publicly available thinking.

The consulting industry now has to prove where human judgment actually matters. The parts that cannot prove it will get repriced. The parts tied to accountability, power, implementation, and institutional permission will survive.

Final compression: 

AI does not kill consulting. 

It kills fake consulting.

以前写过政治评论, 写过六四见证, 也写过诗歌散文, 这一次要写的, 是社会评论. 是我对於一些社会问题的思考. 书名暂定為《一个温和而坚定的社会》. 先分享自序. 全书预计年底在台湾出版发行.

自序

这本小书，集合的是我的一些关於社会问题的思考。没有什麼理论，也算不上什麼宏大叙事。我的原则就是两个: 回归人性，回归常识。因為我发现，或者说我担心，我们的理论和现实，越来越远离人性，远离常识。

我的理想社会，是一个温和而坚定的社会。所谓温和，指的是不管是什麼样的理论、政策或者是运动，都不要走极端。近代以来的历史中，人类社会反反覆覆经历来自左右两个极端的冲击和洗刷，很多人，在很多层次上，已经不再知道什么是温和，取而代之的是仇恨、是斗争、是自认為真理在手的道德优越感。在我看来，这些都是破坏理想社会的毒药。在本书中，我或许拿不出什么药方，但希望可以呈现出一些症状。

所谓坚定，指的是在我们的社会中，应当坚决地排除一些不应该有的政策、行為、思想以及方法，坚决地维护一些应当有的原则、态度、立场和规范。之所以要坚定，是因為这样的排除和维护，需要经过时间的检验，也就是说，不管在怎样的时空环境下，都是不可放弃的。我们应当知道，一个理想社会，不是一个用伪善和利谥衡量一切的社会，也不是一个一切都要用理性来裁决的社会，有些常识，应当是不证自明的公理。

我的这本书，基本上就是在以上两个框架内的思考。我当然不是想充当思想导师，更不认為我的观点就一定是正确的。我只是提出我的一些观察和思考。我以為，这是我们对我们所处的时代应当尽的一点点责任。
